slides.title: Derivatives as local lines
slides.text: Session 1 Derivatives as local lines Explain a derivative as the slope of the best local linear approximation Compute derivatives by rule, with symbolic algebra and with finite differences Choose a finite-difference step by weighing truncation against rounding error 01

slides.title: A derivative is the slope a secant settles on as the gap closes
slides.text: Block 1 · What a derivative is A derivative is the slope a secant settles on as the gap closes The slope between x and x + h is (f(x + h) - f(x)) / h. Shrink h: for a smooth function the slope settles on one number, f′(x). h slope of x² at 3 1 7 0.1 6.1 0.01 6.01 limit 6 Read it as a rate f′(x) is how fast f changes per unit of x, right at x: enrolments per extra thousand of budget, loss per unit change of a weight.

slides.title: The derivative gives the best straight-line fit near a point
slides.text: Block 1 · The definition that generalises The derivative gives the best straight-line fit near a point Local linear approximation f(x + h) ≈ f(x) + f′(x) · h The error shrinks faster than h: halve the step and the error falls to about a quarter. No other straight line through (x, f(x)) does that. This, not "slope of a curve", is the definition that carries to many variables in week 2. Why machine learning cares Training changes weights by small steps. Near the current weights, the loss changes by about derivative × step. Every optimiser in weeks 5 to 8 starts from that line.

slides.title: District D3's enrolment curve and its tangent at 12 thousand
slides.text: Block 1 · In the case District D3's enrolment curve and its tangent at 12 thousand Synthetic: E(x) = 45 · ln(1 + x / 8), drawn by labs/_tools/make_figures.py. 2.25 enrolments per extra thousand at x = 12 E′(x) = 45 / (8 + x), so E′(12) = 45 / 20. The tangent says 2 more thousand bring 4.5 enrolments; the curve gives 4.3.

slides.text: Checkpoint 1 What does the slope promise the finance officer? District D2's curve has E(15) = 50 enrolments and E′(15) = 1.8 per thousand. slides.title: Five rules cover every function in this course
slides.text: Block 2 · Computing derivatives exactly Five rules cover every function in this course Rule Statement Example Power (xⁿ)′ = n xⁿ⁻¹ (x³)′ = 3x² Exponential and log (eˣ)′ = eˣ, (ln x)′ = 1/x (e^(0.5x))′ = 0.5 e^(0.5x) Sum and constant (a f + b g)′ = a f′ + b g′ (4x² - x)′ = 8x - 1 Product (f g)′ = f′ g + f g′ (x eˣ)′ = (1 + x) eˣ Chain f(g(x))′ = f′(g(x)) · g′(x) ln(1 + x/8)′ = 1 / (8 + x) Sigmoid. σ(z) = 1 / (1 + e⁻ᶻ) has σ′(z) = σ(z)(1 - σ(z)): you will use it every week.

slides.title: Symbolic algebra applies the same rules exactly, and can bloat
slides.text: Block 2 · Rules, done by a program Symbolic algebra applies the same rules exactly, and can bloat import sympy as sp x = sp.symbols("x", real=True) g = sp.exp(sp.Rational(1, 2) * x) * x**2 dg = sp.diff(g, x) print(sp.factor(dg)) # x*(x + 4)*exp(x/2)/2 f = sp.lambdify(x, dg, "numpy") print(f(1.0)) # 4.1218... Exact No step size, no rounding until you evaluate. Good for checking a hand derivation. Expression swell Differentiate a long composition symbolically and the formula can grow far larger than the program that computes it. Reverse mode (week 4) avoids that.

slides.title: Add the curvature term and the approximation reaches further
slides.text: Block 2 · Taylor expansions Add the curvature term and the approximation reaches further Taylor, to second order f(x + h) ≈ f(x) + f′(x) h + ½ f″(x) h² The first neglected term is of order h³. The sign of f″ says which side of the tangent the curve lies on. f″ < 0 (concave): the tangent overestimates. f″ > 0 (convex): it underestimates. Extra budget, D3 from 12 Tangent off by 2 thousand 0.5% 5 thousand 2.4% 10 thousand 7.2% 20 thousand 19.1%

slides.title: Which side of the tangent is the curve on?
slides.text: Checkpoint 2 Which side of the tangent is the curve on? A completion-rate curve r(h) of weekly hours h has r″(h) < 0 for every h. The analyst uses the tangent line at h = 3 to predict r at h = 6. What can you say before computing anything? The prediction is too low The prediction is exact It depends on which side of 3 we predict The prediction is too high

slides.title: Finite differences need only the function, and pay with error
slides.text: Block 3 · Derivatives from values alone Finite differences need only the function, and pay with error Forward (f(x + h) - f(x)) / h Truncation error about h/2 · |f″|: first order. Central (f(x + h) - f(x - h)) / (2h) The h² terms cancel: error about h²/6 · |f‴|, second order. Their real job Nobody trains a model with finite differences: one extra evaluation per weight is far too slow. They are the referee: every gradient you derive or code in this course is checked against a central difference.

slides.title: A float holds about 16 digits, and subtraction throws them away
slides.text: Block 3 · The second error A float holds about 16 digits, and subtraction throws them away Machine epsilon, 64-bit: 2.2 × 10⁻¹⁶, the relative gap between neighbouring floats. For tiny h, f(x + h) and f(x) share most digits; their difference keeps the noisy ones. Dividing by h magnifies the noise: rounding error ≈ ε |f| / h. >>> import numpy as np >>> np.finfo(float).eps 2.220446049250313e-16 >>> (1.0 + 1e-16) - 1.0 0.0 What goes wrong. A gradient check with h = 1e-14 "fails" for a correct gradient. The check is broken, not the gradient.

slides.title: Error falls with h, then rises: the best step sits in the V
slides.text: Block 3 · Two errors, one best step Error falls with h, then rises: the best step sits in the V g(x) = e^(0.5x) at x = 1, steps from 0.1 to 1e-12; labs/_tools/make_figures.py. Theory This example Best forward step √ε ≈ 1.5e-8 3e-8 Best central step ∛ε ≈ 6.1e-6 3e-6 Lowest error, forward 6e-9 Lowest error, central 5e-13

slides.title: Which step should the gradient check use next?
slides.text: Checkpoint 3 Which step should the gradient check use next? A colleague checks a hand-coded derivative with a forward difference. With h = 1e-14 the mismatch is 1e-2; with h = 1e-3 it is 1e-4. She concludes the derivative is wrong. Which step should she try first? A forward step near 1e-8 A forward step of 1e-16 A forward step of 1e-1 A central step of 1e-14

slides.title: Gradients and Jacobians
slides.text: Session 1 Gradients and Jacobians Compute partial derivatives and assemble the gradient of a function of several variables Explain the gradient as the direction of steepest increase and a Jacobian as the best local linear map Check a hand-derived gradient or Jacobian with central differences and a relative-error tolerance 01

slides.title: A partial derivative freezes every input but one
slides.text: Block 1 · Partial derivatives A partial derivative freezes every input but one For f(u, v), the partial ∂f/∂u is the week 1 derivative of u ↦ f(u, v) with v held fixed. Geometrically: slice the surface along the u-direction and take the slope of the slice. Example f(u, v) = u² v + e^v ∂f/∂u = 2uv, ∂f/∂v = u² + e^v What goes wrong Forgetting that the frozen input is still in the formula. In ∂f/∂u = 2uv, the value of v matters: the slope along u differs from slice to slice.

slides.title: In a logistic model every partial shares the factor σ(1 - σ)
slides.text: Block 1 · In a model In a logistic model every partial shares the factor σ(1 - σ) r(u, v) = sigmoid(3*u + 2*v - 2.5) dr/du = 3 * r * (1 - r) dr/dv = 2 * r * (1 - r) # at (u, v) = (0.45, 0.45): r = 0.438 # dr/du = 0.738, dr/dv = 0.492 The ratio is the weights' dr/du ÷ dr/dv = 3 ÷ 2 at every point. The size is the curve's σ(1 - σ) is largest, 0.25, where r = 0.5, and near 0 when the model is sure. Sure models learn slowly: week 7.

slides.title: Which partial derivative follows?
slides.text: Checkpoint 1 Which partial derivative follows? A model p = σ(3a + 0.4h - 2) gives a learner p = 0.5, and the analyst computes ∂p/∂h = 0.1 for that learner. What is ∂p/∂a for the same learner? 0.1 3 0.25 0.75

slides.title: The gradient turns week 1's line into a plane
slides.text: Block 2 · The gradient The gradient turns week 1's line into a plane Local linear approximation, n inputs f(x + δ) ≈ f(x) + ∇f(x) · δ ∇f = (∂f/∂x₁, …, ∂f/∂xₙ): one number per input, stacked into a vector. The dot product adds the effect of each input's change, as if each acted alone. Near x that is accurate. Directional derivative The rate of change along a unit vector u is ∇f · u. For the re-enrolment model at (0.45, 0.45): along u alone 0.738; along (0.6, 0.8) it is 0.837.

slides.title: The gradient points uphill, across the level sets
slides.text: Block 2 · Direction of steepest increase The gradient points uphill, across the level sets r(u, v) = σ(3u + 2v - 2.5), a parallel example; labs/_tools/make_figures.py. ∇f · u = |∇f| cos θ: largest when u points along ∇f. The largest rate is |∇f|: 0.887 at (0.45, 0.45). Along a level set f does not change, so the gradient is perpendicular to it. Descent. −∇f is the steepest way down: week 5.

slides.title: Which small change raises the score most?
slides.text: Checkpoint 2 Which small change raises the score most? At (0.45, 0.45) the re-enrolment model has gradient (0.738, 0.492). You may change (u, v) by a step of length 0.1. Which step raises r the most? (0.1, 0) (0.071, 0.071) (0.083, 0.055) (0, 0.1)

slides.title: A Jacobian stacks one gradient per output
slides.text: Block 3 · Several outputs A Jacobian stacks one gradient per output For F: ℝⁿ → ℝᵐ, the Jacobian J is m × n: row i is ∇Fᵢ, entry (i, j) is ∂Fᵢ/∂xⱼ. Local linear map F(x + δ) ≈ F(x) + J δ A matrix times a vector, as in FND-MTH-101: J is the best linear map near x. The district map Five budgets in, five enrolment counts out. Each district depends only on its own budget, so every off-diagonal entry is 0: J is diagonal, with kᵢ / (sᵢ + xᵢ) on the diagonal.

slides.title: The Jacobian predicts a budget shift well when the shift is small
slides.text: Block 3 · Using a Jacobian The Jacobian predicts a budget shift well when the shift is small Split (40, 30, 20, 15, 15); move from D2 to D5 Jacobian predicts Model gives 5 thousand -4.19 -4.72 15 thousand -12.57 -17.98 Diagonal of J at this split: 1.20, 1.24, 1.61, 0.60, 0.40 enrolments per thousand. What goes wrong. Trusting a linear prediction for a large move. Both curves bend, so the error grows faster than the move.

slides.title: Check every coordinate with central differences and a relative error
slides.text: Block 3 · Checking a gradient Check every coordinate with central differences and a relative error def rel_err(g, g_num): return norm(g - g_num) / max(norm(g), norm(g_num)) # g_num[i] = (f(x + h e_i) - f(x - h e_i)) / (2h) # h = 1e-6, one pair of evaluations per input Relative error Read it as below 1e-7 correct 1e-7 to 1e-2 suspicious: a kink, a large step, or a small slip above 1e-2 a wrong formula Look per coordinate. One wrong entry among correct ones points at one formula.

slides.title: What does this gradient check say?
slides.text: Checkpoint 3 What does this gradient check say? A three-parameter gradient is checked with central differences, h = 1e-6. The relative errors of the components are 2e-10, 0.4 and 3e-10. What is the most likely cause? The formula for the second component is wrong The step h is too small for float64 The gradient is fine; the errors are rounding Central differences cannot check this function

slides.title: Any formula a program computes is a graph of simple operations
slides.text: Block 1 · Computational graphs Any formula a program computes is a graph of simple operations f(x, y) = (x + y) · y inputs x = 2, y = 3 ↓ a = x + y a = 5 ↓ f = a · y f = 15 One node per operation, an edge from each input to its use. Each node knows only its local derivatives: for a · y, they are y and a. y is used twice: by the sum and by the product. The forward pass evaluates nodes in an order where inputs come first.

slides.title: Along a chain, multiply the local derivatives
slides.text: Block 1 · The chain rule, scalar Along a chain, multiply the local derivatives A chain x → u = g(x) → f(u) df/dx = f′(u) · g′(x) Example: f = ln(1 + e^(2x)) at x = 0: u = 1 + e^(2x) = 2; df/du = 1/u = 0.5; du/dx = 2 e^(2x) = 2; so df/dx = 1. Two paths: add When an input reaches the output along several paths, the derivative is the sum over paths of the products along each. In (x + y) · y, y has two paths.

slides.title: Go down the graph once, passing adjoints to inputs
slides.text: Block 1 · A backward pass Go down the graph once, passing adjoints to inputs Node Value Local derivative to its inputs Adjoint ∂f/∂node f = a · y 15 to a: y = 3; to y: a = 5 1 a = x + y 5 to x: 1; to y: 1 1 · 3 = 3 x 2 3 · 1 = 3 y 3 1 · 5 + 3 · 1 = 8 Accumulate. y's adjoint is the sum of what each user sends it. Overwriting instead of adding is the classic engine bug.

slides.title: What is the adjoint of the reused input?
slides.text: Checkpoint 1 What is the adjoint of the reused input? In g = u · v with u = 2w and v = w + 1, at w = 3 the values are u = 6, v = 4. What is dg/dw? 8 6 14 48

slides.title: Forward mode carries one tangent up with the values
slides.text: Block 2 · Forward mode Forward mode carries one tangent up with the values Pick one input direction. Each node computes its value and its tangent, d node / d input, from its inputs' tangents. (x + y) · y, tangent along x Value Tangent x, y 2, 3 1, 0 a = x + y 5 1 f = a · y 15 1 · 3 + 5 · 0 = 3 One pass, one direction A forward pass gives the derivative of every output along one input direction: one column of the Jacobian. For the full gradient of f you need a pass per input.

slides.title: Reverse mode wins when many inputs feed one output, as a loss does
slides.text: Block 2 · Which mode Reverse mode wins when many inputs feed one output, as a loss does Function Forward passes Backward passes n inputs, m outputs (full Jacobian) n m A loss of a million weights 1,000,000 1 A curve: one input, many outputs 1 many The price of reverse mode. The backward pass needs every value of the forward pass, so they are kept in memory until it runs. Saved activations are why training needs more memory than prediction.

slides.title: Which mode should the analyst use?
slides.text: Checkpoint 2 Which mode should the analyst use? The analyst needs how all 600 learners' predicted completion chances change with the single attendance threshold the charity sets. One input, 600 outputs. Which costs fewer passes? Reverse mode, one backward pass per learner Forward mode, one pass along the threshold Either: they always cost the same Central differences instead of either mode

slides.title: A logistic loss is four nodes per learner
slides.text: Block 3 · Backpropagation by hand A logistic loss is four nodes per learner z = w · x + b the score → p = σ(z) the chance → ℓ = −[y ln p + (1 − y) ln(1 − p)] the loss → L = mean of ℓ over learners Edge Local derivative ℓ to p −y/p + (1 − y)/(1 − p) p to z p (1 − p) ℓ to z, the product of the two p − y z to wⱼ, to b xⱼ, 1

slides.title: Forward up, backward down: a worked example
slides.text: Block 3 · One learner, worked Forward up, backward down: a worked example x = (0.5, 1.0), y = 1; w = (0.8, −0.4), b = 0.2 Value z = 0.4 − 0.4 + 0.2 0.2 p = σ(0.2) 0.5498 ℓ = −ln 0.5498 0.5981 Backward Adjoint z: p − y −0.4502 w₁: −0.4502 · 0.5 −0.2251 w₂: −0.4502 · 1.0 −0.4502 b: −0.4502 · 1 −0.4502 For two learners, each learner sends its own adjoints and the mean node halves them: a weight's gradient is the average of the learners' pushes.

slides.title: Do it by hand once, carefully, and check it against numbers

Rounding early shows up as a relative error near 1e-3. Check as you go After the forward pass, the code's values; after the backward pass, a numerical gradient check. slides.title: For vector functions, the chain rule multiplies Jacobians
slides.text: Block 1 · The chain rule with vectors For vector functions, the chain rule multiplies Jacobians Composition J(F∘G)(x) = J_F(G(x)) · J_G(x) Shapes chain like the maps: (m × k) · (k × n) = m × n. Matrix products as composition of maps, from FND-MTH-101. A network is a long composition: L = ℓ(f₃(f₂(f₁(x)))). Two orders of multiplying Forward : start at the input, J₃ (J₂ (J₁ v)), one direction v at a time. Reverse: start at the loss, ((gᵀ J₃) J₂) J₁, with gᵀ a row vector. Same product, very different cost.

slides.title: A layer never builds its Jacobian; it passes a vector-Jacobian product
slides.text: Block 1 · What a backward pass passes A layer never builds its Jacobian; it passes a vector-Jacobian product Operation Upstream g = ∂L/∂y Sends back Sum, y = a + b g g to a, g to b Elementwise, y = f(x) vector g g ⊙ f′(x) Dot, y = w · x number g g x to w, g w to x Matrix–vector, y = A x vector g to x: Aᵀg; to A: g xᵀ Tensors. Reverse mode on whole arrays, with broadcasting, is the subject of SPC-DLR-302. This course stays with scalars and small vectors.

slides.title: Each operation returns a node that knows how to pass its gradient back
slides.text: Block 2 · The engine's one idea Each operation returns a node that knows how to pass its gradient back def sqrt(self): s = math.sqrt(self.data) out = Value(s, (self,), "sqrt") def _backward(): # local derivative 1 / (2 sqrt(x)) self.grad += out.grad / (2 * s) out._backward = _backward return out Value : the forward result, computed now. Parents : the inputs, so the graph can be walked. _backward : a closure that remembers what it needs (here s). += : a node may receive from several users.

slides.title: backward() visits nodes in reverse topological order
slides.text: Block 2 · Walking the graph backward() visits nodes in reverse topological order 1 · Order list every node after its inputs → 2 · Seed the output's grad = 1 → 3 · Reverse call each node's _backward, last to first Why the order A node may pass its gradient on only after every user has sent its share. Reverse topological order guarantees it. Why not recursion A recursive sort fails on a chain deeper than Python's recursion limit (about 1,000). The test suite has a 5,000-node chain: use a loop and a stack.

slides.title: What goes wrong in this backward pass?
slides.text: Checkpoint 2 What goes wrong in this backward pass? An engine calls every node's _backward in the order the nodes were created (inputs first), after setting the output's grad to 1. What do the inputs end with? The correct gradients Zero, or only part of their gradient The correct gradients with flipped signs An error about the graph's order

slides.title: Step against the gradient, by a rate you choose
slides.text: Block 1 · Gradient descent Step against the gradient, by a rate you choose The update w ← w − η ∇L(w) From week 2: −∇L is the steepest way down, and the local line promises a fall of about η |∇L|². The promise holds only while the step is small enough for the line to be right. The rate η decides that. What goes wrong A rate that is too small wastes thousands of steps; one that is too large overshoots the valley and climbs out of it. Neither shows in the code: both show in the loss curve.

slides.title: On a quadratic, each direction shrinks by |1 − η λ| per step
slides.text: Block 1 · How large is too large On a quadratic, each direction shrinks by |1 − η λ| per step For L = ½ Σ λᵢ uᵢ², one step multiplies each uᵢ by 1 − η λᵢ. Stable when every |1 − η λᵢ| < 1, that is η < 2 / λ_max. Slow when η λ_min is tiny: the flattest direction barely moves. Near the edge, 1 − η λ_max is close to −1: the steep direction flips sign every step. 0.5 (u² + 10 v²), λ_max = 10, edge at η = 0.2; labs/_tools/make_figures.py.

slides.title: Which rates will the analyst see diverge?
slides.text: Checkpoint 1 Which rates will the analyst see diverge? A least-squares loss has curvatures (eigenvalues of AᵀA / n) from 0.05 to 4. The analyst sweeps the rate over 0.01, 0.1, 0.4 and 0.6 with full-batch gradient descent. Which runs diverge? 0.1, 0.4 and 0.6 0.4 and 0.6 0.6 only None of them

slides.title: A mini-batch gradient is cheap, right on average, and noisy
slides.text: Block 2 · Stochastic and mini-batch gradients A mini-batch gradient is cheap, right on average, and noisy The loss is a mean over n rows, so its gradient is a mean too. A random batch of b rows gives an unbiased estimate at b / n of the cost. Many cheap steps per pass over the data (an epoch), instead of one exact step. The noise does not vanish at the minimum: with a fixed rate, the weights keep moving. Batch size as a dial b = 1 is stochastic gradient descent in its first form; b = n is full batch. Larger b: less noise per step, more cost per step. The lab uses b = 32.

slides.title: Momentum keeps a velocity, so the flat direction speeds up
slides.text: Block 2 · Momentum Momentum keeps a velocity, so the flat direction speeds up Heavy ball v ← β v + ∇L(w) w ← w − η v Steps that agree add up, to about η / (1 − β) in a steady slope; steps that flip sign cancel. With β = 0.9 it averages about the last ten gradients. Same quadratic, same rate 0.04, 25 steps: loss 6.5 without momentum, 0.095 with β = 0.8.

slides.title: Adaptive methods scale each coordinate; schedules change the rate over time
slides.text: Block 2 · Adaptive steps and schedules Adaptive methods scale each coordinate; schedules change the rate over time Adaptive step (Adam, for example) Keep running averages of g and g². Step each coordinate by η · m̂ / (√v̂ + ε): about η per coordinate whatever the gradient's scale. Common defaults: β₁ = 0.9, β₂ = 0.999. Warm-up, then decay Warm-up : start small for the first steps, when gradients are large and erratic. Decay: shrink the rate later, to narrow the noise band. Step, cosine and linear decays are all in use. Awareness level. Which adaptive optimiser is in common use changes; AdamW, scaling rules and newer methods are SPC-DLR-302's subject.

slides.title: What does momentum change here?
slides.text: Checkpoint 2 What does momentum change here? Plain gradient descent at its largest stable rate zigzags across a narrow valley and crawls along it. The analyst adds momentum with β = 0.9 and keeps the rate. What should she expect first? Faster progress along the valley, possibly with overshoot; retune the rate Faster progress along the valley, and nothing else A lower final loss than the least-squares solution No change unless the batch size changes

slides.title: Each failure has a shape you can name from the curve
slides.text: Block 3 · Reading loss curves Each failure has a shape you can name from the curve The curve Diagnosis Likely cause First fix Grows, or turns into NaN diverged η above 2 / λ_max divide η by 3 to 10 Falls fast, then crawls far above the best slow η too small for λ_min; unscaled features scale features; raise η; momentum Falls, then a wide band that never narrows noisy small batch at a large constant η decay the rate; larger batch Saw-tooth on the way down near the edge η close to 2 / λ_max lower η a little Smooth fall to the reference converged keep it, and log it

slides.title: Log every run, not only the best one
slides.text: Block 3 · Reporting Log every run, not only the best one variant,learning_rate,seed,epochs_run,final_loss,diagnosis batch,0.5,0,200,...,converged batch,2.0,0,57,inf,diverged A sweep that reports only its best rate hides how fragile the method is. Every run gets its rate, its seed, its result and a diagnosis in words. The capstone is scored on this: every run, seed and failure, not the best result alone.

slides.title: Convexity and curvature
slides.text: Session 1 Convexity and curvature Distinguish convex from non-convex objectives with a test you can run Classify critical points from the eigenvalues of the Hessian Relate the largest stable step to the largest curvature 01

slides.title: A convex function lies below every chord, so it has no traps
slides.text: Block 1 · Convexity A convex function lies below every chord, so it has no traps Definition f(t a + (1 − t) b) ≤ t f(a) + (1 − t) f(b) for all a, b and t in [0, 1] Twice differentiable: convex exactly when f″ ≥ 0 everywhere, or in several variables when the Hessian has no negative eigenvalue anywhere. Why it matters On a convex loss every local minimum is a global minimum, and a small enough step of gradient descent reaches it. Least squares and logistic regression are convex in their weights. A network's loss is not.

slides.title: Non-convex losses have local minima, saddles and plateaus
slides.text: Block 1 · What non-convex looks like Non-convex losses have local minima, saddles and plateaus Local minimum Lower than its neighbours, higher than the best point. Descent stops there. Saddle point Gradient zero, curving up one way and down another. In many dimensions, saddles far outnumber minima. Plateau A wide region where the gradient is close to zero. Steps become tiny; the run looks converged and is not. What goes wrong. Reading "the loss stopped falling" as "we found the minimum". A saddle or a plateau stops the loss too.

slides.title: What does convexity guarantee here?
slides.text: Checkpoint 1 What does convexity guarantee here? The charity's analyst fits a logistic regression twice, from two different starting weights, with a small enough step. Both runs stop. What can she conclude about the two end points? They may be different local minima Both runs reach the same lowest loss Any step size gives the same end point One of them may be a saddle point

slides.title: The Hessian's eigenvalues are the curvatures along its eigenvectors
slides.text: Block 2 · Curvature The Hessian's eigenvalues are the curvatures along its eigenvectors The Hessian H holds the second partial derivatives: Hᵢⱼ = ∂²f / ∂wᵢ∂wⱼ. It is symmetric. Second-order Taylor f(w + d) ≈ f(w) + ∇f · d + ½ dᵀ H d Along an eigenvector with eigenvalue λ, the function curves like ½ λ t². At a critical point, eigenvalues Kind all positive minimum all negative maximum both signs saddle some zero the test cannot tell

slides.title: Exactly on a saddle's ridge, descent stops; a nudge lets it escape
slides.text: Block 2 · Saddles in practice Exactly on a saddle's ridge, descent stops; a nudge lets it escape f = ½x² − ½y² + 0.1y⁴, step 0.2, 120 steps; labs/_tools/make_figures.py. On the axis the y-component of the gradient is exactly 0: descent walks into the saddle at (0, 0). From y = 0.01 it ends at (0, 1.581), a minimum (√2.5). Noise helps. Mini-batch gradients rarely sit exactly on a ridge.

slides.title: What kind of point is this?
slides.text: Checkpoint 2 What kind of point is this? At a point where the gradient of a two-weight loss is zero, the Hessian is [[3, 0], [0, −0.2]]. The run has stopped there. What should the analyst say? It is a minimum, since 3 is large and positive The test cannot tell: −0.2 is too small to count as negative It is a saddle: lower loss lies along the second weight It is a maximum

slides.title: The largest curvature bounds the step; the ratio of curvatures sets the pace
slides.text: Block 3 · Step size and curvature The largest curvature bounds the step; the ratio of curvatures sets the pace Near a minimum the loss is about quadratic with Hessian H: week 5's rule holds with λ_max of H. Step < 2 / λ_max. At the best fixed step, the flattest direction shrinks by about 1 − 2/κ per step, with κ = λ_max / λ_min, the condition number. Steps needed grow roughly in proportion to κ. Lab 5.1, airfoil data κ Raw features 2.7 × 10¹¹ Standardised features 12

slides.title: A Newton step divides by the curvature instead of guessing a rate
slides.text: Block 3 · Using the curvature A Newton step divides by the curvature instead of guessing a rate Newton Solve H d = −∇f, then w ← w + d. On a quadratic it lands on the minimum in one step, whatever κ is. Why not always H has n² entries: for a million weights, a trillion. At a saddle a Newton step goes towards the saddle, not away. Training uses first-order methods; Newton is the yardstick.

slides.title: What will the sweep show?
slides.text: Checkpoint 3 What will the sweep show? A convex quadratic loss has curvatures 0.5 and 50. The analyst runs plain gradient descent at steps 0.01, 0.039 and 0.041. What does she see? 0.041 diverges; the other two converge, slowly along the flat direction All three converge quickly All three converge, since a convex loss cannot diverge whatever the step 0.039 and 0.041 diverge

slides.title: Shift the logits by their maximum before exponentiating
slides.text: Block 1 · Overflow Shift the logits by their maximum before exponentiating A 64-bit float stops at about 1.8 × 10³⁰⁸, so exp(z) is inf for z above about 709.8. A model's logits can reach that. Softmax ignores a common shift softmax(z) = softmax(z − m) for any number m. Take m = max z: the largest exponent is then exp(0) = 1. Logits (3, 1, −1) value exp of the shifted (0, −2, −4) 1, 0.135, 0.018 softmax 0.867, 0.117, 0.016 log-sum-exp = 3 + log(1 + e⁻² + e⁻⁴) 3.143

slides.title: Compute cross-entropy from logits, never as the log of a probability
slides.text: Block 1 · The loss Compute cross-entropy from logits, never as the log of a probability Stable form CE(z, y) = logsumexp(z) − z_y No probability is formed, so no probability can round to 0. Fragile form −log(softmax(z)_y) If the probability of the label rounds to 0, the loss is inf and every gradient after it is nan. In practice. Libraries offer a loss that takes logits for exactly this reason; pass it logits, not probabilities.

slides.title: Which computation is safe?
slides.text: Checkpoint 1 Which computation is safe? A model gives the logits (900, 905) for a learner with label 0. Which way of computing the cross-entropy returns a finite, correct number in 64-bit floats? Take −log of exp(900) / (exp(900) + exp(905)) Clip both logits to 709, then use the naive formula Compute 905 + log(e⁻⁵ + 1) − 900 Divide both logits by 905, then use the naive formula

slides.title: The gradient of softmax cross-entropy is probabilities minus the label
slides.text: Block 2 · The gradient The gradient of softmax cross-entropy is probabilities minus the label The Jacobian of softmax is ∂pᵢ/∂zⱼ = pᵢ (δᵢⱼ − pⱼ): diag(p) − p pᵀ. Differentiate logsumexp(z) − z_y directly: the first term gives p, the second gives the one-hot vector e_y. Result ∂CE / ∂z = p − e_y Logits (2, 0, 1), label 2 value p 0.665, 0.090, 0.245 e_y 0, 0, 1 gradient p − e_y 0.665, 0.090, −0.755

slides.title: What is the gradient?
slides.text: Checkpoint 2 What is the gradient? For one learner the model's probabilities are (0.1, 0.7, 0.2) and the true level is 0. What is the gradient of the cross-entropy with respect to the three logits? (0.1, −0.3, 0.2) (0.9, −0.7, −0.2) (−10, 0, 0) (−0.9, 0.7, 0.2)

slides.title: On separable data the plain loss falls for ever; a penalty gives it a minimum
slides.text: Block 3 · Penalties On separable data the plain loss falls for ever; a penalty gives it a minimum Four points x = −2, −1, 1, 2 with labels 0, 0, 1, 1; labs/_tools/make_figures.py. Any c > 0 classifies all four points; a larger c is more confident, and the loss is lower. No finite c is best. Penalised loss L(w) + (λ/2) ‖w‖² Minimum at c = 2.43 for λ = 0.02, and at c = 1.46 for λ = 0.1.

slides.title: The penalty adds λ to every curvature, so the minimum becomes unique
slides.text: Block 3 · What the penalty changes The penalty adds λ to every curvature, so the minimum becomes unique Hessian H + λI: every eigenvalue rises by λ. A convex loss becomes strictly convex, with one minimiser. Gradient ∇L + λw: each step also shrinks the weights by the factor 1 − ηλ, which is why it is called weight decay. Price The minimiser is no longer the plain loss's best point: the training loss rises. Whether held-out loss falls is a measurement, not a promise.

slides.title: What does the penalty do to this Hessian?
slides.text: Checkpoint 3 What does the penalty do to this Hessian? At its minimum, a plain loss in two weights has Hessian eigenvalues 0 and 4. The analyst adds the penalty (0.5/2)‖w‖². What are the new eigenvalues, and what changes? 0.5 and 4.5: the minimiser is now unique 0 and 2: the steep direction is flattened 0.5 and 4: only the flat direction changes 0 and 4: a penalty only moves the minimum

slides.title: At a constrained optimum, the gradient points across the constraint
slides.text: Block 1 · The Lagrangian At a constrained optimum, the gradient points across the constraint Maximise f(x) subject to g(x) = c. Moving along the constraint cannot improve f, so ∇f is parallel to ∇g: Lagrange conditions ∇f = λ ∇g and g(x) = c Equivalently: set the derivatives of f − λ (g − c) to zero. Maximise 2 log x + log y, x + y = 6 value conditions: 2 / x = λ, 1 / y = λ x = 2y constraint: 3y = 6 y = 2, x = 4 multiplier λ = 0.5

slides.title: The multiplier is the price of the constraint: value per extra unit
slides.text: Block 1 · The multiplier The multiplier is the price of the constraint: value per extra unit Reading If the best value is V(c), then dV/dc = λ. One more unit of budget is worth about λ units of the objective, for small changes. In the example λ = 0.5: raising the total from 6 to 6.1 adds about 0.05 to the best value. Its units are the objective's units per unit of the constraint. Why it matters. A finance officer asks "what would another thousand buy?" The multiplier answers without re-solving.

slides.title: What does the multiplier say?
slides.text: Checkpoint 1 What does the multiplier say? A training team's best accuracy under a compute limit of 100 hours has multiplier λ = 0.002 accuracy points per hour. The limit is cut to 90 hours. What should the team expect? Accuracy falls by 0.002 Accuracy falls by about 0.02 Accuracy is unchanged and λ rises Accuracy falls by 0.0002

slides.title: With budgets that cannot be negative, a programme can get nothing
slides.text: Block 2 · Limits that bind With budgets that cannot be negative, a programme can get nothing Three programmes, value k log(1 + x/s), budget 30; labs/_tools/make_figures.py. Each funded programme gets x = k/λ − s: where its margin meets λ. C's margin at zero is 0.8, below λ = 1.163: its first unit is worth less than the last unit anywhere else, so x_C = 0. Find λ by bisection: raise it until the budgets fit.

slides.title: Projected gradient: step uphill, then return to the nearest allowed point
slides.text: Block 2 · A second way Projected gradient: step uphill, then return to the nearest allowed point v = x + η ∇f(x): an ordinary gradient step. x = project(v): the nearest point with x ≥ 0 and sum = budget, which is max(v − θ, 0) for one θ. Repeat until x stops moving. Week 5 applies Too small a step crawls; too large a step overshoots and never settles. Both solutions should agree; if they do not, one of them is wrong.

slides.title: Who gets funded?
slides.text: Checkpoint 2 Who gets funded? At the optimum of an allocation, λ = 1.5. A fourth programme has margin k / s = 1.2 at zero budget. What should it receive? An equal share of the budget Enough budget to raise its margin up to λ = 1.5 first 1.5 units of budget Nothing: its first unit is worth less than λ

slides.title: Optimising a convenient proxy can harm the people a model serves
slides.text: Block 3 · Responsible use Optimising a convenient proxy can harm the people a model serves The proxy One number that is easy to count and maximise. The optimiser does exactly what it is told, including leaving out whoever the number does not see. The fix is a decision A floor, or weights by need, changes the answer. Which one, and how much, is policy: the mathematics prices it, it does not choose it. Separate the roles The analyst proposes options with their prices; the finance officer approves the budget; the programme lead decides the weights.

slides.title: Who decides?
slides.text: Checkpoint 3 Who decides? An analyst finds that adding a floor for two programmes costs 0.6 units of the objective per unit of budget. Which next step keeps the duties separate? Present both options with their prices to the person who sets the weights Adopt the floor, since it is fairer Drop the floor, since it lowers the objective Approve the cheaper option now and tell the finance officer afterwards
